solution: The body starts from rest with a constant acceleration \(a\), so its speed grows linearly, \(v = at\). The acceleration is constant, so by Newton's second law the force is constant too, \(F = ma\). The instantaneous power is the product of the two: \(P = Fv = (ma)(at) = ma^{2}t\). Since \(m\) and \(a\) are both constant, the power is directly proportional to \(t\). The key point is that only ONE of the two factors in \(P = Fv\) grows with time here — the force does not.

The power is constant, so \(P = Fv = m\dfrac{dv}{dt}v\) is a constant. Separating the variables, \(v\,dv = \dfrac{P}{m}\,dt\), and integrating from rest gives \(\dfrac{v^{2}}{2} = \dfrac{P}{m}t\), so \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2P}{m}}\,t^{1/2}\) — the speed rises as \(t^{1/2}\), not linearly, because a constant power delivers less force as the body speeds up. Integrating once more for the displacement, \(x = \int v\,dt \propto \int t^{1/2}\,dt \propto t^{3/2}\). So the displacement grows as \(t^{3/2}\).
